title: Reviewing code is a skill
excerpt: A discussion on code review with short case studies and links to research on expertise.
content_html:
Intended audience: Software developers interested in getting better at developing software. Initially, I meant this post more for junior developers, but some parts are more applicable for tech leads etc. So if the post appears a bit muddled, please accept this apology from my inner Pascal, “Sorry, I did not have the time to break it up into two posts.”

In developer communities, there has been a lot of discussion on code review, especially over the course of 2025-2026. For example, you may have seen claims like:Not necessarily all from the same people.

  1. “Code review is the bottleneck”
  2. “Mandatory pre-merge code review is for low-trust environments; you should push directly to main”
  3. “Code review doesn’t find bugs”
  4. “Code review is not for X, it’s for Y”
  5. “LLMs are better than humans at reviewing code”
  6. “LLM code reviews are much better than humans at finding edge cases/bugs”
  7. “You should stop looking at the code; you should be doing XYZ instead”

and so on.

Out of this, zooming in on “Code review is not for X, it’s for Y” for a moment, the research has the following to say:

By coding our interview data, we identified four key themes for what Google developers expect from code reviews: education, maintaining norms, gatekeeping, and accident prevention. Education regards either teaching or learning from a code review and is in line with the initial reasons for introducing code review; norms refer to an organization preference for a discretionary choice (e.g., formatting or API usage patterns); gatekeeping concerns the establishment and maintenance of boundaries around source code, design choices or another artifact; and accidents refer to the introduction of bugs, defects or other quality related issues.

– Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google (2018)

Similarly, Expectations, outcomes, and challenges of modern code review (2013) points out:

Our study reveals that while finding defects remains the main motivation for review, reviews are less about defects than expected and instead provide additional benefits such as knowledge transfer, increased team awareness, and creation of alternative solutions to problems. Moreover, we find that code and change understanding is the key aspect of code reviewing and that developers employ a wide range of mechanisms to meet their understanding needs, most of which are not met by current tools

So at least, hopefully we can agree that code review serves many purposes.

I will get to the other points in a bit.

But before that, I want to articulate a framing which I haven’t seen much elsewhere. Namely, that reviewing code is a skill. Specifically, I posit that:

  • It’s possible to get better at reviewing code. By “better”, I mean across all of the purposes above: catching bugs, catching design issues, increasing one’s awareness of what’s going on, and understanding the code.
  • It’s possible to teach someone to get better at reviewing code.
  • By virtue of it being a fairly modern skill, we don’t quite know where the human skill ceiling lies (e.g. what is the Pareto frontier in terms of speed vs quality?).
  • If you’re a software developer, and if you believe that people will continue to be involved in the development and maintenance of programs for the foreseeable future, then it’s valuable to get better at reviewing code.

First, I will give three small examples taken from the past few weeks of work of me finding bugs when reviewing code. I’ve specifically chosen bugs for discussion because they’re relatively unambiguous.

Next, I will provide some of my own historical background related to code review, and some arguments in favor of the core thesis.

After that, I discuss some ideas for experimenting with and improving code review.

Finally, I discuss the aforementioned oft-repeated memes around code review and how they hold up to scrutiny with the thesis in mind.

Let’s get started.

A tale of three almost-introduced bugs

A bunch of details have been elided in the course of explaining the different examples below, in an attempt to make them digestible. It may be valuable to keep an eye on stray thoughts of the form, “well, that seems like a code smell, no wonder you almost had that bug” or “duh, this could’ve been avoided with XYZ”.

In two out of the three cases, the person who wrote the PR had experience with the surrounding code.

The other thing to note is that LLM reviews with a mixture of high-end coding models (around Jun 2026) were run for all of the PRs described below. They did not catch the issues that I caught.

It may be helpful to consult this handy table from Lorin Hochstein’s Traditional versus resilience engineering views:The post is short and recommended reading. The table below is a subset of the one in the original post.

Traditional view focuses on Resilience engineering view focuses on
objectives production pressure
reducing complexity navigating complexity
root cause interaction of multiple factors
human variability as liability human variability as asset

One way to read the cases below is to try to think about both sides of the table as you read them.

Writing some git configuration

We use our own devboxesDisposable VMs used for software development. at $WORK which run on EC2 instances. The logic for starting things has two subprocesses:

  • One background process, to initialize state which isn’t needed right away. This process may or may not have finished by the time the user starts using the devbox.

  • One foreground process, which needs some extra data from the user’s laptop, and blocks the user until it’s done. Only after this process finishes can the user start using the devbox.

To reduce latency, we’ve been working on moving more operations to the background process. In this spirit, one of my colleagues created a PR to move some of the modifications to the global ~/.gitconfigIn the interest of performance and consistency, we want to manage some aspects of people’s Git configurations. Yes, I know Nix exists, I use it for one of my own servers. No, we don’t use Nix at work. You’re keeping a check on your intrusive thoughts, right? from the foreground process to the background process.

So when a git config command needs to modify ~/.gitconfig, it first acquires an exclusive file lock on ~/.gitconfig.lock. This prevents concurrent modifications from other (cooperating) processes, such as other git config calls.

When I saw the PR, I remembered we’d hit non-determinism in the devbox setup, where git’s behavior of fast-failure on lock acquisition failure led to flakiness during startup due to a similar problem of concurrent writes.

Just retrying on top would’ve still led to non-determinism, so my colleague added a cross-process dependency edge using an existing mechanism, where the write would only happen after the background process finished.

Then I pointed out that we’d actually tried that earlier, but we’d gotten rid of that almost immediately, due to the increase in end-to-end latency (because now a subpart of the foreground process would have to wait for the whole background process to finish).

In the end, since we also had some file modifications which couldn’t quite go through git config directly,Due to needing to reconcile # DO NOT EDIT blocks. we converged on a solution which had a separate flock operation (with its own .lock file). This allowed for (1) having retries with backoff (2) doing multiple modifications under the same flock without other intervening writes (3) doing direct writes without worrying about concurrent writers.

To display progress or not to display progress

There’s a periodic CI job which does some processing and uploads a tarball to an AWS S3 bucket. Turns out, the aws CLI displays progress by default. Presumably, this is meant to help with debugging issues, as well as provide reassurance about progress when using the CLI directly in the terminal.

When this colleague changed the logic to upload to 4 buckets from 1 bucket to speed up downloads from other regions,AWS buckets belong to a specific region. the CI job started failing, due to the log file exceeding the limit of 10MB.

Turns out, the aws CLI logs a line for every 256 KB uploaded. This corresponds to tens of thousands of log lines when the upload is 10GB+. Multiplying the log lines by 4 tipped the job over the 10MB limit.

The colleague submitted a PR to change the invocations to use --no-progress to unbork the CI job. At the time, my first thought was, “Hmm, is this the only option? Maybe there’s a way to show fewer progress updates? If the job fails mid-upload, it’d be nice to have some progress information to make it clearer when the job failed relative to the start of the upload.”

So I looked up the docs for the aws CLI, and saw a flag --progress-seconds <INT> which allowed tuning the frequency of progress updates. I asked the PR author if we could use that instead.

At the back of my mind, I remembered a mini-incident we’d had earlier, where a commonly used script had introduced an aws CLI flag, but not all environments the script ran in had a sufficiently new CLI version which supported it, so the script broke for a bunch of people.

Since the PR author had also seen that happen, I assumed that they would do the due diligence to check what version of the CLI was running in the CI job and check whether that CLI version supported --progress-seconds.

The PR author got back to me quickly and updated the PR to remove --no-progress and use --progress-seconds.

I was a bit surprised at the speed, so I realized they might not have thought of the same risk. First, I tried looking at the aws CLI changelog to see if it mentioned when the flag was introduced (since the flag’s documentation didn’t have this information). It did not. Then I had LLM chase down what CLI version the CI job was using, as well as which commit introduced that flag in the aws CLI, and the first published release with that commit. This uncovered the fact that the job would break if --progress-seconds was used, because the existing CLI version in the job was too old.

I did some spot checks on the commits and versions, and then commented on the PR with a brief apology for not stating my assumptions earlier, and asked if they could cross-check the findings/find an alternate solution.

The PR was later fixed by installing a sufficiently new aws CLI version that was already being packaged in another place in the repo.

Remember the CI job from the previous example? One of the things I’ve been working on lately is decoupling the release process of that job group from the overall CI release process.The CI system is complicated enough that different jobs can have their own release processes.

One day, I hit a merge conflict while rebasing my WIP changes on top of the master branch. Turns out, someone had added new variations of the existing job.

So the job group is responsible for uploading certain tarballs. An engineer needed some more tarballs to be uploaded slightly differently. They’d created a separate job for that, instead of updating an existing job in the group.

I was like, “hmm, why is this a different job, shouldn’t it involve adding one more element to a list somewhere?”

Turns out, the reviewer for that job-addition PR had recommended separating out the new job from the old one to start with to reduce risk with disrupting the existing job’s performance, reliability etc. Additionally, one of the “slight” differences was that the new job was uploading sidecar files with a checksum.If you’re reading this and going “but doesn’t S3 already natively support checksums”, I actually didn’t know about that until after all of this was done-and-dusted, and I’m guessing the original PR author didn’t either.

I was confused looking at that. “If this job needs checksums, do the existing jobs need checksums? If so, why didn’t they make the checksum logic uniformly applicable to all jobs? Do we need to update the existing readers to check the integrity of the old tarballs? Are these new tarballs crossing some kind of trust boundary whereas the old tarballs were not?”

Thinking a bit more, I realized there was a bug. About a year back, I’d watched a presentation by Prof. Hannes Mühleisen called DuckLake - The SQL-Powered Lakehouse Format for the Rest of Us. It was talking about Apache Iceberg and its use of files, which seemed very complicated.

At the time, my understanding was that some of this complexity was due to essentially not having a way to do multi-object transactions. And thus, one of the key design decisions for DuckLake was to have a SQL database (with ACID transactions) for maintaining metadata.

Coming back to the CI job, it was uploading the tarball to a fixed object name in a fixed bucket. This was uploaded before the checksum. So while S3 guarantees all-or-nothing semantics for a write to an object, if the job was canceled or crashed before uploading the checksum, then readers checking the integrity of the tarball against the old checksum in a fail-closed mannerThe usual way to use checksums. would start failing, which would lead to an ~outage for that particular feature until the tarball and checksums were back in sync.

I pointed out this failure mode to the person who created the PR, as well as in the PR introducing the read path. In the end, the read path check for the sidecar file was not introduced.

The case for code review being a skill

Let’s rewind the clock back a bit. To 2018.

I was working as a graduate student in physics. The research I was doing involved various kinds of simulations. We used Jupyter notebooks for much of the work. The simulations would work one day, they’d stop working the next day, and the third day, they’d continue not working despite undoing the work from the second day.

I was struggling with how to manage the code, how to make it efficient, and how to prevent mistakes from coming up, and how to use version control. At the time, I started learning about automated testing and code review. I recall being quite amazed, “Wait, what? People actually review all of the code, not just the outputs?! Wow, it must be nice to work as a software developer.”

Eventually, I got increasingly more interested in the process of writing software better, and more disenchanted with the physics I was supposed to be studying. I ended up dropping out of the PhD program in 2019, and started working as a software engineer.

Since then until now, over the course of my career so far, there have been multiple times where someone have commented that they’ve found my code reviews more helpful than the average review they’re used to.

As one data point, before 2026, when reviewing a PR, depending on the author’s familiarity with how I review, the underlying code, prior discussions etc., my comment density on PRs has been in the range of 30-100 SLOC/comment. Not all of them were about bugs. Most were about more “boring” things like asking clarifying questions, naming, layering etc.

So why am I telling you all of this? Well, my point is that I learnt how to review code along the way. I was not magically born with some innate ability to do code review, or to catch bugs in code review.

Are there aspects somewhat specific to me which help me in spotting bugs? Probably, yes. Some things I can think of:

  • When I discover a bug that I introduced earlier, I tend to take it more personally than other developers I’ve met.
  • I tend to think of programs in terms of invariants and little proofs.
  • I like reading tech blogs and watching tech talks, especially those with debugging stories and performance investigations.

Out of these, I think the second point in particular is very learnable and teachable.

Stepping back a bit, I think there’s a lot we don’t really know about code review. If you look at the literature on code reviews, it’s generally pretty anemic.

Apart from doing more structured studies – which would be difficult to get buy-in for in a typical corporate environment – I think there’s a lot of room for trying out new practices related to code review, including at small scales, to make it more useful for authors, reviewers and the surrounding team.

Putting on the mad scientist hat for a bit

In this section, I want to suggest some potential ideas to improve upon (or at least, try variations of) code review as a practice. The purpose of writing these down is twofold:

  • To give you some inspiration for coming up with ideas of your own.
  • To give you some sense of how existing practices are lacking in particular aspects

The point is not “you should go try these out” (maybe you shouldn’t) or “I am certain that these will work well” (I’m not, because I haven’t had the chance to put them into practice).

The ideas below assume a strong foundation of psychological safety, because if you don’t have that, you should almost certainly be fixing that first before trying out more weird things.

Randomized process-oriented Socratic dialogues

Say you have a junior engineer who is requesting a review from a senior engineer with expertise relevant to the code being changed.

When the PR is up, and the review is requested, say a bot randomly decides (based on some tunable frequency) to create a meeting.

In the meeting, the senior person, instead of pointing out things which don’t quite make sense, or could be done differently, instead first asks the junior person for their perspective on why they did things a certain way, or what assumptions they were making.It’s key to avoid counterfactual questions for why something was not done a certain way, or why the person did not think of something. This might sound easy, but if you actually try this, you’ll notice it’s quite hard to stick to this!

During this process, a junior with cognitive agility will recognize gaps in their understanding, and potentially identify improvements they could make.

The focus would be on the thought process for different sub-skills like writing a good PR description or robust error handling, with the PR serving as a foil to ground the discussion.

See also: 6 principles of Effective feedback, §1. Effective feedback is based on process, not outcome.

Lightweight near-miss post-mortems

Today, it’s increasingly more common to have post-mortems for incidents. It’s also common to organize work into sprints and have team retro meetings at the end of a sprint.Also a skill that can be learned, improved upon etc.!

What if, every time a bug was caught in code review during the sprint, the PR author was asked to record a short clip explaining the context and what the caught issue was, and if the kind of issue matched a past issue, what the impact of the past issue was.The wording here is very deliberate. I’m explicitly not mentioning “what the potential impact could’ve been had the issue slipped through” because that goes into the territory of speculation/prediction.

During the team retro, the team could watch the clips together, ask questions and increase shared knowledge. This way, everyone on the team would also be exposed to a lot more bugs that almost slipped through.

To avoid having differences in frequency, you could limit this to at most one clip per person per meeting.

See also: You’re missing your near misses.

Firewalled modeling

In Finding bugs without running or even looking at code (video) (StrangeLoop 2019), Jay Parlar describes an example of him trying to build a model in Alloy for an access control system – which spanned multiple codebases, and where he hadn’t looked at the code – and in the process of modeling, he found both bugs and design issues.

In my own limited experience, lightweight formal methods seem useful when trying to reason about process semantics (involving cancelation, potentially indefinite waits, file locking protocols) as well as access control.

What if, as a baseline, when you started working on a system, especially a complex one which interfaced with multiple external systems or carried high security or correctness risks, two people played the roles of the modeler and the programmer. The modeler would develop the model without looking at the code, and the programmer would work on the code. They’d meet in the middle to create test cases.

Then the model could serve as a much smaller reference to be able to review the thoroughness of the code, as well as to test out various unusual situations that would otherwise require a large amount of test scaffolding, especially in the early stages of the project.

Studying expertise

(OK, this one doesn’t fit under “mad scientist” but whatever. It’s my blog.)

In many fields, there is a growing body of literature around expertise. This doesn’t really exist for code (and specifically code review) in quite the same way.

What if you analyzed the code reviews happening in your team and tried to figure out if there are outlier (domain, person) pairs in terms of insightful review comments. Or maybe you get this information just from interviewing people.

Once you’ve found the outliers, you could try an easy-to-learn approach like Applied Cognitive Task Analysis for extracting the tacit knowledge these people have. Doing this is easier for code review compared to many other tasks, because instead of simulating a difficult-to-simulate situation (such as firefighting), you can actually just have the person review PRs live.

On the zeitgeist surrounding code review

Hopefully, by this point, I’ve convinced you somewhat that reviewing code is a skill, and that there’s a lot more room left for us to try out different practices. For example, in terms of training programs, we are not close to more well-studied areas like team sports (e.g. soccer) and two-player games (like Chess, Go etc.).

At this point, you might (reasonably) still be thinking: “So what? LLMs are going to get better at all of these things much faster than humans can get better at them, so it’s pointless to try to compete with LLMs at reviewing code.”A related objection might be that while you might care about code review, your management doesn’t. Sorry, I don’t have any advice related to convincing management.

If you’ll recall my phrasing from before:

If you’re a software developer, and if you believe that people will continue to be involved in the development and maintenance of programs for the foreseeable future, then it’s valuable to get better at reviewing code.

The second part of this is conditional on the first. So we can disagree on what likelihood we assign to the premise itself (“if you believe … for the foreseeable future”) being true, but that’s a separate discussion from whether the implication (the “then”) itself holds.

The flipped version of the implication would be something like:

If you’re a software developer, and even if you believe that people will continue to be involved in the development and maintenance of programs for the foreseeable future, it’s net negative to get better at reviewing code.

For example, you could hold this position because you think that there are other skills which you could learn that provide significantly higher leverage.I commonly see “system design” and “product thinking” or “developing taste” as being touted as more important to develop. Or you might think that reviewing code will later be restricted to a small fraction of working programmers, like how a relatively small fraction of programmers today look at assembly code on a regular basis.

To this, I have the following responses.

First, if you’re able to drop down a lower-level of abstraction compared to your peers, that’s almost always an advantage because you’re able to tackle a wider set of problems that they can. For example, today, if you’re able to understand SQL query plans more easily, or you understand things like memory allocation and assembly, you are at an advantage at designing more robust and high-performance code compared to engineers who don’t understand those topics.

Second, given that software development is still in its infancy compared to so many other fields, it’s quite possible that we’re not even close to seeing the ceiling on human skill and performance on various aspects, such as, but not limited to, code review. So it may very well be that the average skill you see around you may be far from the ceiling is.

Lastly, I recommend grounding your world view in experience reports, case studies, and your own observations, rather than “takes” on social media. Cedric Chin has written about much better about this than I could’ve in How to make sense of AI and Letter to a young person worrying about AI.

At the end of the day, if you’re going to be responsible for the code you ship, and the code you ship has real consequences for real people, it’s worth asking how you can get better at what you do. To that end, I believe that investing in getting better at reviewing code is one of the best things you can do as a software developer.

Yaksha: What is swifter than the wind?

Yudhishtira: The mind.

Yaksha: More numerous than the blades of grass?

Yudhishtira: The thoughts in the mind.

Yaksha: What is the most praiseworthy thing of all?

Yudhishtira: Skill.

Yaksha: The most valuable possession?

Yudhishtira: Knowledge.

One of the things I’ve been working on lately is decoupling the release process of that job group from the overall CI release process.The CI system is complicated enough that different jobs can have their own release processes. One day, I hit a merge conflict while rebasing my WIP changes on top of the master branch. Turns out, someone had added new variations of the existing job. So the job group is responsible for uploading certain tarballs. An engineer needed some more tarballs to be uploaded slightly differently. They’d created a separate job for that, instead of updating an existing job in the group. I was like, “hmm, why is this a different job, shouldn’t it involve adding one more element to a list somewhere?” Turns out, the reviewer for that job-addition PR had recommended separating out the new job from the old one to start with to reduce risk with disrupting the existing job’s performance, reliability etc. Additionally, one of the “slight” differences was that the new job was uploading sidecar files with a checksum.If you’re reading this and going “but doesn’t S3 already natively support checksums”, I actually didn’t know about that until after all of this was done-and-dusted, and I’m guessing the original PR author didn’t either. I was confused looking at that. “If this job needs checksums, do the existing jobs need checksums? If so, why didn’t they make the checksum logic uniformly applicable to all jobs? Do we need to update the existing readers to check the integrity of the old tarballs? Are these new tarballs crossing some kind of trust boundary whereas the old tarballs were not?” Thinking a bit more, I realized there was a bug. About a year back, I’d watched a presentation by Prof. Hannes Mühleisen called DuckLake - The SQL-Powered Lakehouse Format for the Rest of Us. It was talking about Apache Iceberg and its use of files, which seemed very complicated. At the time, my understanding was that some of this complexity was due to essentially not having a way to do multi-object transactions. And thus, one of the key design decisions for DuckLake was to have a SQL database (with ACID transactions) for maintaining metadata. Coming back to the CI job, it was uploading the tarball to a fixed object name in a fixed bucket. This was uploaded before the checksum. So while S3 guarantees all-or-nothing semantics for a write to an object, if the job was canceled or crashed before uploading the checksum, then readers checking the integrity of the tarball against the old checksum in a fail-closed mannerThe usual way to use checksums. would start failing, which would lead to an ~outage for that particular feature until the tarball and checksums were back in sync. I pointed out this failure mode to the person who created the PR, as well as in the PR introducing the read path. In the end, the read path check for the sidecar file was not introduced. The case for code review being a skill Let’s rewind the clock back a bit. To 2018. I was working as a graduate student in physics. The research I was doing involved various kinds of simulations. We used Jupyter notebooks for much of the work. The simulations would work one day, they’d stop working the next day, and the third day, they’d continue not working despite undoing the work from the second day. I was struggling with how to manage the code, how to make it efficient, and how to prevent mistakes from coming up, and how to use version control. At the time, I started learning about automated testing and code review. I recall being quite amazed, “Wait, what? People actually review all of the code, not just the outputs?! Wow, it must be nice to work as a software developer.” Eventually, I got increasingly more interested in the process of writing software better, and more disenchanted with the physics I was supposed to be studying. I ended up dropping out of the PhD program in 2019, and started working as a software engineer. Since then until now, over the course of my career so far, there have been multiple times where someone have commented that they’ve found my code reviews more helpful than the average review they’re used to. As one data point, before 2026, when reviewing a PR, depending on the author’s familiarity with how I review, the underlying code, prior discussions etc., my comment density on PRs has been in the range of 30-100 SLOC/comment. Not all of them were about bugs. Most were about more “boring” things like asking clarifying questions, naming, layering etc. So why am I telling you all of this? Well, my point is that I learnt how to review code along the way. I was not magically born with some innate ability to do code review, or to catch bugs in code review. Are there aspects somewhat specific to me which help me in spotting bugs? Probably, yes. Some things I can think of: When I discover a bug that I introduced earlier, I tend to take it more personally than other developers I’ve met. I tend to think of programs in terms of invariants and little proofs. I like reading tech blogs and watching tech talks, especially those with debugging stories and performance investigations. Out of these, I think the second point in particular is very learnable and teachable. Stepping back a bit, I think there’s a lot we don’t really know about code review. If you look at the literature on code reviews, it’s generally pretty anemic. Apart from doing more structured studies – which would be difficult to get buy-in for in a typical corporate environment – I think there’s a lot of room for trying out new practices related to code review, including at small scales, to make it more useful for authors, reviewers and the surrounding team. Putting on the mad scientist hat for a bit In this section, I want to suggest some potential ideas to improve upon (or at least, try variations of) code review as a practice. The purpose of writing these down is twofold: To give you some inspiration for coming up with ideas of your own. To give you some sense of how existing practices are lacking in particular aspects The point is not “you should go try these out” (maybe you shouldn’t) or “I am certain that these will work well” (I’m not, because I haven’t had the chance to put them into practice). The ideas below assume a strong foundation of psychological safety, because if you don’t have that, you should almost certainly be fixing that first before trying out more weird things. Randomized process-oriented Socratic dialogues Say you have a junior engineer who is requesting a review from a senior engineer with expertise relevant to the code being changed. When the PR is up, and the review is requested, say a bot randomly decides (based on some tunable frequency) to create a meeting. In the meeting, the senior person, instead of pointing out things which don’t quite make sense, or could be done differently, instead first asks the junior person for their perspective on why they did things a certain way, or what assumptions they were making.It’s key to avoid counterfactual questions for why something was not done a certain way, or why the person did not think of something. This might sound easy, but if you actually try this, you’ll notice it’s quite hard to stick to this! During this process, a junior with cognitive agility will recognize gaps in their understanding, and potentially identify improvements they could make. The focus would be on the thought process for different sub-skills like writing a good PR description or robust error handling, with the PR serving as a foil to ground the discussion. See also: 6 principles of Effective feedback, §1. Effective feedback is based on process, not outcome. Lightweight near-miss post-mortems Today, it’s increasingly more common to have post-mortems for incidents. It’s also common to organize work into sprints and have team retro meetings at the end of a sprint.Also a skill that can be learned, improved upon etc.! What if, every time a bug was caught in code review during the sprint, the PR author was asked to record a short clip explaining the context and what the caught issue was, and if the kind of issue matched a past issue, what the impact of the past issue was.The wording here is very deliberate. I’m explicitly not mentioning “what the potential impact could’ve been had the issue slipped through” because that goes into the territory of speculation/prediction. During the team retro, the team could watch the clips together, ask questions and increase shared knowledge. This way, everyone on the team would also be exposed to a lot more bugs that almost slipped through. To avoid having differences in frequency, you could limit this to at most one clip per person per meeting. See also: You’re missing your near misses. Firewalled modeling In Finding bugs without running or even looking at code (video) (StrangeLoop 2019), Jay Parlar describes an example of him trying to build a model in Alloy for an access control system – which spanned multiple codebases, and where he hadn’t looked at the code – and in the process of modeling, he found both bugs and design issues. In my own limited experience, lightweight formal methods seem useful when trying to reason about process semantics (involving cancelation, potentially indefinite waits, file locking protocols) as well as access control. What if, as a baseline, when you started working on a system, especially a complex one which interfaced with multiple external systems or carried high security or correctness risks, two people played the roles of the modeler and the programmer. The modeler would develop the model without looking at the code, and the programmer would work on the code. They’d meet in the middle to create test cases. Then the model could serve as a much smaller reference to be able to review the thoroughness of the code, as well as to test out various unusual situations that would otherwise require a large amount of test scaffolding, especially in the early stages of the project. Studying expertise (OK, this one doesn’t fit under “mad scientist” but whatever. It’s my blog.) In many fields, there is a growing body of literature around expertise. This doesn’t really exist for code (and specifically code review) in quite the same way. What if you analyzed the code reviews happening in your team and tried to figure out if there are outlier (domain, person) pairs in terms of insightful review comments. Or maybe you get this information just from interviewing people. Once you’ve found the outliers, you could try an easy-to-learn approach like Applied Cognitive Task Analysis for extracting the tacit knowledge these people have. Doing this is easier for code review compared to many other tasks, because instead of simulating a difficult-to-simulate situation (such as firefighting), you can actually just have the person review PRs live. On the zeitgeist surrounding code review Hopefully, by this point, I’ve convinced you somewhat that reviewing code is a skill, and that there’s a lot more room left for us to try out different practices. For example, in terms of training programs, we are not close to more well-studied areas like team sports (e.g. soccer) and two-player games (like Chess, Go etc.). At this point, you might (reasonably) still be thinking: “So what? LLMs are going to get better at all of these things much faster than humans can get better at them, so it’s pointless to try to compete with LLMs at reviewing code.”A related objection might be that while you might care about code review, your management doesn’t. Sorry, I don’t have any advice related to convincing management. If you’ll recall my phrasing from before: If you’re a software developer, and if you believe that people will continue to be involved in the development and maintenance of programs for the foreseeable future, then it’s valuable to get better at reviewing code. The second part of this is conditional on the first. So we can disagree on what likelihood we assign to the premise itself (“if you believe … for the foreseeable future”) being true, but that’s a separate discussion from whether the implication (the “then”) itself holds. The flipped version of the implication would be something like: If you’re a software developer, and even if you believe that people will continue to be involved in the development and maintenance of programs for the foreseeable future, it’s net negative to get better at reviewing code. For example, you could hold this position because you think that there are other skills which you could learn that provide significantly higher leverage.I commonly see “system design” and “product thinking” or “developing taste” as being touted as more important to develop. Or you might think that reviewing code will later be restricted to a small fraction of working programmers, like how a relatively small fraction of programmers today look at assembly code on a regular basis. To this, I have the following responses. First, if you’re able to drop down a lower-level of abstraction compared to your peers, that’s almost always an advantage because you’re able to tackle a wider set of problems that they can. For example, today, if you’re able to understand SQL query plans more easily, or you understand things like memory allocation and assembly, you are at an advantage at designing more robust and high-performance code compared to engineers who don’t understand those topics. Second, given that software development is still in its infancy compared to so many other fields, it’s quite possible that we’re not even close to seeing the ceiling on human skill and performance on various aspects, such as, but not limited to, code review. So it may very well be that the average skill you see around you may be far from the ceiling is. Lastly, I recommend grounding your world view in experience reports, case studies, and your own observations, rather than “takes” on social media. Cedric Chin has written about much better about this than I could’ve in How to make sense of AI and Letter to a young person worrying about AI. At the end of the day, if you’re going to be responsible for the code you ship, and the code you ship has real consequences for real people, it’s worth asking how you can get better at what you do. To that end, I believe that investing in getting better at reviewing code is one of the best things you can do as a software developer. Yaksha: What is swifter than the wind? Yudhishtira: The mind. By coding our interview data, we identified four key themes for what Google developers expect from code reviews: education, maintaining norms, gatekeeping, and accident prevention. – Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google (2018)

blocks.html_en: So when a git config command needs to modify ~/.gitconfig, it first acquires an exclusive file lock on ~/.gitconfig.lock. This prevents concurrent modifications from other (cooperating) processes, such as other git config calls.

sentences.en: This prevents concurrent modifications from other (cooperating) processes, such as other git config calls.
sentences.zh: 这可以防止其他（协作）进程的并发修改，例如其他 git config 调用。

blocks.html_en: When I saw the PR, I remembered we’d hit non-determinism in the devbox setup, where git’s behavior of fast-failure on lock acquisition failure led to flakiness during startup due to a similar problem of concurrent writes.

sentences.en: When I saw the PR, I remembered we’d hit non-determinism in the devbox setup, where git’s behavior of fast-failure on lock acquisition failure led to flakiness during startup due to a similar problem of concurrent writes.
sentences.zh: 当我看到 PR 时，我记得我们在 devbox 设置中遇到了非确定性，其中 git 在锁定获取失败时的快速失败行为导致启动期间由于类似的并发写入问题而不稳定。

blocks.html_en: Just retrying on top would’ve still led to non-determinism, so my colleague added a cross-process dependency edge using an existing mechanism, where the write would only happen after the background process finished.

sentences.en: Just retrying on top would’ve still led to non-determinism, so my colleague added a cross-process dependency edge using an existing mechanism, where the write would only happen after the background process finished.
sentences.zh: 仅在顶部重试仍然会导致不确定性，因此我的同事使用现有机制添加了跨进程依赖边缘，其中写入仅在后台进程完成后才会发生。

blocks.html_en: Then I pointed out that we’d actually tried that earlier, but we’d gotten rid of that almost immediately, due to the increase in end-to-end latency (because now a subpart of the foreground process would have to wait for the whole background process to finish).

sentences.en: Then I pointed out that we’d actually tried that earlier, but we’d gotten rid of that almost immediately, due to the increase in end-to-end latency (because now a subpart of the foreground process would have to wait for the whole background process to finish).
sentences.zh: 然后我指出，我们实际上之前已经尝试过这一点，但由于端到端延迟的增加，我们几乎立即摆脱了这一点（因为现在前台进程的子部分必须等待整个后台进程完成）。

sentences.en: The case for code review being a skill

blocks.html_en: Let’s rewind the clock back a bit. To 2018.

sentences.en: Let’s rewind the clock back a bit.
sentences.zh: 让我们把时钟拨回一点。

blocks.html_en: I was working as a graduate student in physics. The research I was doing involved various kinds of simulations. We used Jupyter notebooks for much of the work. The simulations would work one day, they’d stop working the next day, and the third day, they’d continue not working despite undoing the work from the second day.

sentences.en: I was working as a graduate student in physics.
sentences.zh: 我当时是一名物理学研究生。

sentences.en: The research I was doing involved various kinds of simulations.
sentences.zh: 我所做的研究涉及各种模拟。

sentences.en: We used Jupyter notebooks for much of the work.
sentences.zh: 我们使用 Jupyter Notebook 来完成大部分工作。

sentences.en: The simulations would work one day, they’d stop working the next day, and the third day, they’d continue not working despite undoing the work from the second day.
sentences.zh: 模拟有一天会起作用，第二天就会停止工作，第三天，尽管撤消了第二天的工作，但它们仍会继续不工作。

blocks.html_en: I was struggling with how to manage the code, how to make it efficient, and how to prevent mistakes from coming up, and how to use version control. sentences.en: I was struggling with how to manage the code, how to make it efficient, and how to prevent mistakes from coming up, and how to use version control.
sentences.zh: 我一直在努力解决如何管理代码、如何提高代码效率、如何防止出现错误以及如何使用版本控制。

sentences.en: At the time, I started learning about automated testing and code review.
sentences.zh: 当时，我开始学习自动化测试和代码审查。

sentences.en: I recall being quite amazed, “Wait, what?
sentences.zh: 我记得当时我很惊讶：“等等，什么？

sentences.en: People actually review all of the code, not just the outputs?!
sentences.zh: 人们实际上审查了所有代码，而不仅仅是输出？！

sentences.en: Wow, it must be nice to work as a software developer.”
sentences.zh: 哇，作为一名软件开发人员工作一定很愉快。”

blocks.html_en: Eventually, I got increasingly more interested in the process of writing software better, and more disenchanted with the physics I was supposed to be studying. I ended up dropping out of the PhD program in 2019, and started working as a software engineer.

sentences.en: Eventually, I got increasingly more interested in the process of writing software better, and more disenchanted with the physics I was supposed to be studying.
sentences.zh: 最终，我对更好地编写软件的过程越来越感兴趣，并对我应该学习的物理不再抱有幻想。

sentences.en: I ended up dropping out of the PhD program in 2019, and started working as a software engineer.
sentences.zh: 我最终于 2019 年放弃了博士课程，开始担任软件工程师。

blocks.html_en: Since then until now, over the course of my career so far, there have been multiple times where someone have commented that they’ve found my code reviews more helpful than the average review they’re used to.

sentences.en: Since then until now, over the course of my career so far, there have been multiple times where someone have commented that they’ve found my code reviews more helpful than the average review they’re used to.
sentences.zh: 从那时起到现在，在我迄今为止的职业生涯中，曾多次有人评论说他们发现我的代码审查比他们习惯的平均审查更有帮助。

blocks.html_en: As one data point, before 2026, when reviewing a PR, depending on the author’s familiarity with how I review, the underlying code, prior discussions etc., my comment density on PRs has been in the range of 30-100 SLOC/comment. Not all of them were about bugs. Most were about more “boring” things like asking clarifying questions, naming, layering etc.

sentences.en: As one data point, before 2026, when reviewing a PR, depending on the author’s familiarity with how I review, the underlying code, prior discussions etc., my comment density on PRs has been in the range of 30-100 SLOC/comment.
sentences.zh: 作为一个数据点，在 2026 年之前，在审查 PR 时，根据作者对我的审查方式、底层代码、之前的讨论等的熟悉程度，我对 PR 的评论密度一直在 30-100 SLOC/评论之间。

sentences.en: Not all of them were about bugs.
sentences.zh: 并非所有这些都与错误有关。

sentences.en: Most were about more “boring” things like asking clarifying questions, naming, layering etc.
sentences.zh: 大多数都是关于更“无聊”的事情，比如提出澄清问题、命名、分层等。

blocks.html_en: So why am I telling you all of this? Well, my point is that I learnt how to review code along the way. I was not magically born with some innate ability to do code review, or to catch bugs in code review.

sentences.en: So why am I telling you all of this?
sentences.zh: 那么我为什么要告诉你这一切呢？

sentences.en: Well, my point is that I learnt how to review code along the way.
sentences.zh: 好吧，我的观点是我一路上学会了如何审查代码。

sentences.en: I was not magically born with some innate ability to do code review, or to catch bugs in code review.
sentences.zh: 我并不是神奇地生来就有进行代码审查或在代码审查中发现错误的天生能力。

blocks.html_en: Are there aspects somewhat specific to me which help me in spotting bugs? Probably, yes. Some things I can think of:

sentences.en: Are there aspects somewhat specific to me which help me in spotting bugs?
sentences.zh: 是否有一些特定的方面可以帮助我发现错误？

sentences.en: Probably, yes.
sentences.zh: 可能是的。

sentences.en: Some things I can think of:
sentences.zh: 我能想到的一些事情：

blocks.html_en: • When I discover a bug that I introduced earlier, I tend to take it more personally than other developers I’ve met.

sentences.en: When I discover a bug that I introduced earlier, I tend to take it more personally than other developers I’ve met.
sentences.zh: 当我发现之前引入的错误时，我倾向于比我遇到的其他开发人员更个人化。

blocks.html_en: • I tend to think of programs in terms of invariants and little proofs.

sentences.en: I tend to think of programs in terms of invariants and little proofs.
sentences.zh: 我倾向于从不变量和少量证明的角度来考虑程序。

blocks.html_en: • I like reading tech blogs and watching tech talks, especially those with debugging stories and performance investigations.

sentences.en: I like reading tech blogs and watching tech talks, especially those with debugging stories and performance investigations.
sentences.zh: 我喜欢阅读技术博客和观看技术讲座，尤其是那些包含调试故事和性能调查的博客。

blocks.html_en: Out of these, I think the second point in particular is very learnable and teachable.

sentences.en: Out of these, I think the second point in particular is very learnable and teachable.
sentences.zh: 其中，我认为第二点特别值得学习和传授。

blocks.html_en: Stepping back a bit, I think there’s a lot we don’t really know about code review. If you look at the literature on code reviews, it’s generally pretty anemic.

sentences.en: Stepping back a bit, I think there’s a lot we don’t really know about code review.
sentences.zh: 退一步来说，我认为关于代码审查我们还有很多不了解的地方。

sentences.en: If you look at the literature on code reviews, it’s generally pretty anemic.
sentences.zh: 如果你看一下有关代码审查的文献，你会发现它通常相当贫乏。

blocks.html_en: Apart from doing more structured studies – which would be difficult to get buy-in for in a typical corporate environment – I think there’s a lot of room for trying out new practices related to code review, including at small scales, to make it more useful for authors, reviewers and the surrounding team.

sentences.en: Apart from doing more structured studies – which would be difficult to get buy-in for in a typical corporate environment – I think there’s a lot of room for trying out new practices related to code review, including at small scales, to make it more useful for authors, reviewers and the surrounding team.

blocks.html_en: Putting on the mad scientist hat for a bit

sentences.en: Putting on the mad scientist hat for a bit
sentences.zh: 暂时戴上疯狂科学家的帽子

blocks.html_en: In this section, I want to suggest some potential ideas to improve upon (or at least, try variations of) code review as a practice. The purpose of writing these down is twofold:

sentences.en: In this section, I want to suggest some potential ideas to improve upon (or at least, try variations of) code review as a practice.
sentences.zh: 在本节中，我想提出一些潜在的想法，以改进（或至少尝试其变体）代码审查作为实践。

sentences.en: The purpose of writing these down is twofold:
sentences.zh: 写下这些内容的目的有两个：

blocks.html_en: • To give you some inspiration for coming up with ideas of your own.

sentences.en: To give you some inspiration for coming up with ideas of your own.
sentences.zh: 为您提供一些灵感，帮助您提出自己的想法。

blocks.html_en: • To give you some sense of how existing practices are lacking in particular aspects

sentences.en: To give you some sense of how existing practices are lacking in particular aspects
sentences.zh: 让您了解现有实践在特定方面的不足

blocks.html_en: The point is not “you should go try these out” (maybe you shouldn’t) or “I am certain that these will work well” (I’m not, because I haven’t had the chance to put them into practice).

sentences.en: The point is not “you should go try these out” (maybe you shouldn’t) or “I am certain that these will work well” (I’m not, because I haven’t had the chance to put them into practice).
sentences.zh: 重点不是“你应该去尝试这些”（也许你不应该）或“我确信这些会很好用”（我不是，因为我还没有机会将它们付诸实践）。

blocks.html_en: The ideas below assume a strong foundation of psychological safety, because if you don’t have that, you should almost certainly be fixing that first before trying out more weird things.

sentences.en: The ideas below assume a strong foundation of psychological safety, because if you don’t have that, you should almost certainly be fixing that first before trying out more weird things.
sentences.zh: 下面的想法假设了心理安全的坚实基础，因为如果你没有这个基础，你几乎肯定应该先解决这个问题，然后再尝试更奇怪的事情。

blocks.html_en: In the meeting, the senior person, instead of pointing out things which don’t quite make sense, or could be done differently, instead first asks the junior person for their perspective on why they did things a certain way, or what assumptions they were making.It’s key to avoid counterfactual questions for why something was not done a certain way, or why the person did not think of something. sentences.en: In the meeting, the senior person, instead of pointing out things which don’t quite make sense, or could be done differently, instead first asks the junior person for their perspective on why they did things a certain way, or what assumptions they were making.It’s key to avoid counterfactual questions for why something was not done a certain way, or why the person did not think of something.

content_html_zh:
目标受众：有兴趣更好地开发软件的软件开发人员。 最初，我的意思是这篇文章更适合初级开发人员，但有些部分更适用于技术主管等。因此，如果这篇文章看起来有点混乱，请接受我内心 Pascal 的道歉，“抱歉，我没有时间将其分成两篇文章。”

在开发者社区中，关于代码审查的讨论很多，尤其是在 2025-2026 年期间。 例如，您可能见过这样的说法：不一定全部来自同一个人。

  1. “代码审查是瓶颈”
  2. “强制合并前代码审查适用于低信任环境；您应该直接推送到主”
  3. “代码审查没有发现错误”
  4. “代码审查不是针对 X，而是针对 Y”
  5. “法学硕士在审查代码方面比人类更好”
  6. “LLM 代码审查在发现边缘情况/错误方面比人类好得多”
  7. “你不应该再看代码；你应该做 XYZ”

等等。

由此，暂时聚焦于“代码审查不是针对 X，而是针对 Y”，研究结果如下：

通过对采访数据进行编码，我们确定了 Google 开发人员对代码审查的期望的四个关键主题：教育、维护规范、把关和事故预防。 教育关注的是从代码审查中进行教学或学习，并且符合引入代码审查的最初原因；规范是指组织对酌情选择的偏好（例如，格式或 API 使用模式）；把关涉及源代码、设计选择或其他工件周围边界的建立和维护；事故是指错误、缺陷或其他质量相关问题的引入。 – 现代代码审查：Google 案例研究 (2018)

同样，现代代码审查的期望、结果和挑战 (2013) 指出：

我们的研究表明，虽然发现缺陷仍然是审查的主要动机，但审查与预期相比较少涉及缺陷，而是提供了额外的好处，例如知识转移、提高团队意识以及创建问题的替代解决方案。 此外，我们发现代码和变更理解是代码审查的关键方面，开发人员采用多种机制来满足他们的理解需求，其中大部分是当前工具无法满足的

因此，至少，希望我们能够同意代码审查有多种用途。

我稍后会讨论其他要点。

但在此之前，我想阐明一个我在其他地方没见过的框架。 也就是说，审查代码是一项技能。 具体来说，我认为：

  • 可以更好地审查代码。 我所说的“更好”是指涵盖上述所有目的：捕获错误、捕获设计问题、提高对正在发生的事情的认识以及理解代码。
  • 教某人更好地审查代码是可能的。
  • 由于它是一项相当现代的技能，我们不太知道人类技能的上限在哪里（例如，速度与质量的帕累托边界是什么？）。
  • 如果您是一名软件开发人员，并且您相信在可预见的将来人们将继续参与程序的开发和维护，那么更好地审查代码就很有价值。

首先，我将给出三个小例子，这些例子取自我过去几周在检查代码时发现错误的工作。 我专门选择了错误进行讨论，因为它们相对明确。

接下来，我将提供一些我自己与代码审查相关的历史背景，以及一些支持核心论文的论点。

之后，我讨论了一些尝试和改进代码审查的想法。

最后，我讨论了前面提到的关于代码审查的经常重复的模因，以及它们如何经得起论文的审查。

让我们开始吧。

编写一些 git 配置

我们使用自己的 devboxes 一次性虚拟机用于软件开发。 在 EC2 实例上运行的 $WORK。 启动事物的逻辑有两个子流程：

  • 一个后台进程，用于初始化不需要立即使用的状态。 当用户开始使用 devbox 时，此过程可能已经完成，也可能尚未完成。
  • 一个前台进程需要来自用户笔记本电脑的一些额外数据，并会阻止用户直到完成为止。 只有此过程完成后，用户才能开始使用 devbox。

为了减少延迟，我们一直致力于将更多操作移至后台进程。 本着这种精神，我的一位同事创建了一个 PR，将一些修改移至全局 ~/.gitconfig。为了性能和一致性，我们希望管理人们的 Git 配置的某些方面。 是的，我知道 Nix 存在，我将它用于我自己的服务器之一。 不，我们在工作中不使用 Nix。 你正在控制自己的侵入性想法，对吗？ 从前台进程到后台进程。

因此，当 git config 命令需要修改 ~/.gitconfig 时，它首先会获取 ~/.gitconfig.lock 上的独占文件锁。 这可以防止其他（协作）进程的并发修改，例如其他 git config 调用。

当我看到 PR 时，我记得我们在 devbox 设置中遇到了非确定性，其中 git 在锁定获取失败时的快速失败行为导致启动期间由于类似的并发写入问题而不稳定。

仅在顶部重试仍然会导致不确定性，因此我的同事使用现有机制添加了跨进程依赖边缘，其中写入仅在后台进程完成后才会发生。

然后我指出，我们实际上之前已经尝试过这一点，但由于端到端延迟的增加，我们几乎立即摆脱了这一点（因为现在前台进程的子部分必须等待整个后台进程完成）。

最后，由于我们还进行了一些无法直接通过 git config 进行的文件修改，因为需要协调 # DO NOT EDIT 块。 我们集中在一个具有单独的集群操作（具有自己的.lock文件）的解决方案上。 这允许 (1) 进行回退重试 (2) 在同一个集群下进行多次修改，而无需其他干预写入 (3) 进行直接写入而不用担心并发写入。

显示进度或不显示进度

有一个定期的 CI 作业，它会进行一些处理并将 tarball 上传到 AWS S3 存储桶。 事实证明，aws CLI 默认显示进度。 据推测，这旨在帮助解决问题，并在直接在终端中使用 CLI 时提供进度保证。

当这位同事更改逻辑从1个存储桶上传到4个存储桶以加快其他区域的下载时，AWS存储桶属于特定区域。 由于日志文件超过 10MB 的限制，CI 作业开始失败。

结果是，aws CLI 每上传 256 KB 就会记录一行。 当上传超过 10GB 时，这相当于数万条日志行。 将日志行乘以 4 会使作业超过 10MB 限制。

这位同事提交了一个 PR，以更改调用以使用 --no-progress 来取消 CI 作业。 当时，我的第一个想法是：“嗯，这是唯一的选择吗？ 也许有办法显示更少的进度更新？ 如果作业在上传过程中失败，最好能提供一些进度信息，以便更清楚地了解相对于上传开始时作业失败的时间。”

因此，我查找了 aws CLI 的文档，并看到了一个标志 --progress-seconds <INT>，它允许调整进度更新的频率。 我问公关作者我们是否可以用它来代替。

在我的脑海深处，我想起了我们之前遇到的一个小事件，其中一个常用的脚本引入了 aws CLI 标志，但并非该脚本运行的所有环境都有支持它的足够新的 CLI 版本，因此该脚本对很多人来说都崩溃了。

由于 PR 作者也看到了这种情况，我认为他们会尽职调查来检查 CI 作业中运行的 CLI 版本，并检查该 CLI 版本是否支持 --progress-seconds。

PR 作者很快回复了我，并更新了 PR 以删除 --no-progress 并使用 --progress-seconds。

我对速度有点惊讶，所以我意识到他们可能没有想到同样的风险。 首先，我尝试查看 aws CLI 变更日志，看看它是否提到了该标志的引入时间（因为该标志的文档没有此信息）。 但事实并非如此。 然后，我让 LLM 追踪 CI 作业使用的 CLI 版本，以及哪个提交在 aws CLI 中引入了该标志，以及该提交的第一个发布版本。 这揭示了这样一个事实：如果使用 --progress-seconds，作业将会中断，因为作业中现有的 CLI 版本太旧。

我对提交和版本进行了一些抽查，然后对 PR 发表了评论，并为没有提前说明我的假设而表示了简短的歉意，并询问他们是否可以交叉检查结果/找到替代解决方案。

后来通过安装足够新的 aws CLI 版本修复了 PR，该版本已打包在存储库的另一个位置。

还记得前面示例中的 CI 作业吗？ 我最近一直在做的事情之一就是将该作业组的发布过程与整个 CI 发布过程解耦。CI 系统足够复杂，不同的作业可以有自己的发布过程。

有一天，我在主分支之上重新调整 WIP 更改时遇到了合并冲突。 事实证明，有人在现有工作的基础上添加了新的变体。

因此工作组负责上传某些 tarball。 工程师需要上传更多的 tarball，但上传方式略有不同。 他们为此创建了一个单独的作业，而不是更新组中的现有作业。

我当时想，“嗯，为什么这是一项不同的工作，它不应该涉及在列表中的某个地方添加一个元素吗？”

事实证明，该新增作业 PR 的审阅者建议首先将新作业与旧作业分开，以降低破坏现有作业性能、可靠性等的风险。此外，其中一个“轻微”差异是新作业正在上传带有校验和的 sidecar 文件。如果您正在阅读本文并继续“但 S3 本身不支持校验和”，实际上我直到所有这些都完成并除尘后才知道这一点，并且我猜最初的公关作者也没有。

看着那个我很困惑。 “如果这个工作需要校验和，那么现有的工作也需要校验和吗？ 如果是这样，为什么他们不让校验和逻辑统一适用于所有作业？ 我们是否需要更新现有的阅读器来检查旧 tarball 的完整性？ 这些新的 tarball 是否跨越了某种信任边界，而旧的 tarball 则没有？”

再想一想，我发现有一个错误。 大约一年前，我观看了 Hannes Mühleisen 教授的演讲，名为 DuckLake - The SQL-Powered Lakehouse Format for the Rest of Us。 讲的是Apache Iceberg以及它对文件的使用，看起来很复杂。

当时，我的理解是，这种复杂性部分是由于本质上没有办法进行多对象事务。 因此，DuckLake 的关键设计决策之一是使用 SQL 数据库（具有 ACID 事务）来维护元数据。

回到 CI 作业，它将 tarball 上传到固定存储桶中的固定对象名称。 这是在校验和之前上传的。 因此，虽然 S3 保证写入对象的“全有或全无”语义，但如果作业在上传校验和之前被取消或崩溃，则读取器会以故障关闭方式（使用校验和的常用方式）根据旧校验和检查 tarball 的完整性。 将开始失败，这将导致该特定功能的中断，直到 tarball 和校验和恢复同步。

我向创建 PR 的人指出了这种失败模式，并在 PR 中介绍了读取路径。 最终没有引入sidecar文件的读取路径检查。

代码审查是一项技能的案例

让我们把时钟拨回一点。 到2018年。

我当时是一名物理学研究生。 我所做的研究涉及各种模拟。 我们使用 Jupyter Notebook 来完成大部分工作。 模拟有一天会起作用，第二天就会停止工作，第三天，尽管撤消了第二天的工作，但它们仍会继续不工作。

我一直在努力解决如何管理代码、如何提高代码效率、如何防止出现错误以及如何使用版本控制。 当时，我开始学习自动化测试和代码审查。 我记得当时我很惊讶：“等等，什么？ 人们实际上审查了所有代码，而不仅仅是输出？！ 哇，作为一名软件开发人员工作一定很愉快。”

最终，我对更好地编写软件的过程越来越感兴趣，并对我应该学习的物理不再抱有幻想。 我最终于 2019 年放弃了博士课程，开始担任软件工程师。

从那时起到现在，在我迄今为止的职业生涯中，曾多次有人评论说他们发现我的代码审查比他们习惯的平均审查更有帮助。

作为一个数据点，在 2026 年之前，在审查 PR 时，根据作者对我的审查方式、底层代码、之前的讨论等的熟悉程度，我对 PR 的评论密度一直在 30-100 SLOC/评论之间。 并非所有这些都与错误有关。 大多数都是关于更“无聊”的事情，比如提出澄清问题、命名、分层等。

那么我为什么要告诉你这一切呢？ 好吧，我的观点是我一路上学会了如何审查代码。 我并不是神奇地生来就有进行代码审查或在代码审查中发现错误的天生能力。

是否有一些特定的方面可以帮助我发现错误？ 可能是的。 我能想到的一些事情：

  • 当我发现之前引入的错误时，我倾向于比我遇到的其他开发人员更个人化。
  • 我倾向于从不变量和少量证明的角度来考虑程序。
  • 我喜欢阅读技术博客和观看技术讲座，尤其是那些包含调试故事和性能调查的博客。

其中，我认为第二点特别值得学习和传授。

退一步来说，我认为关于代码审查我们还有很多不了解的地方。 如果你看一下有关代码审查的文献，你会发现它通常相当贫乏。

除了进行更结构化的研究（这在典型的企业环境中很难获得认可）之外，我认为还有很大的空间来尝试与代码审查相关的新实践（包括小规模的实践），以使其对作者、审阅者和周围团队更有用。

暂时戴上疯狂科学家的帽子

在本节中，我想提出一些潜在的想法，以改进（或至少尝试其变体）代码审查作为实践。 写下这些内容的目的有两个：

  • 为您提供一些灵感，帮助您提出自己的想法。
  • 让您了解现有实践在特定方面的不足

重点不是“你应该去尝试这些”（也许你不应该）或“我确信这些会很好用”（我不是，因为我还没有机会将它们付诸实践）。

下面的想法假设了心理安全的坚实基础，因为如果你没有这个基础，你几乎肯定应该先解决这个问题，然后再尝试更奇怪的事情。

随机过程导向的苏格拉底式对话

假设您有一位初级工程师，他正在请求一位具有与要更改的代码相关的专业知识的高级工程师进行审查。

当 PR 提出并请求审核时，假设机器人随机决定（基于某些可调频率）创建会议。

在会议中，高级人员不会指出不太合理或可以采取不同方式做的事情，而是首先询问初级人员对为什么他们以某种方式做事，或者他们做出什么假设的看法。避免提出反事实的问题，例如为什么某件事没有以某种方式做，或者为什么这个人没有想到某件事，这一点很关键。 这听起来可能很容易，但如果你真正尝试一下，你会发现坚持下去是相当困难的！

在此过程中，具有认知敏捷性的初级人员将认识到他们理解中的差距，并可能发现他们可以做出的改进。

重点将放在不同子技能的思考过程上，例如编写良好的 PR 描述或强大的错误处理，并以 PR 作为讨论的陪衬。

轻量级未遂事件事后分析

如今，对事件进行事后分析变得越来越普遍。 将工作组织成冲刺并在冲刺结束时召开团队回顾会议也很常见。这也是一项可以学习、改进等的技能！

如果每次冲刺期间在代码审查中发现错误时，PR 作者都被要求录制一个短片，解释上下文和发现的问题是什么，如果问题类型与过去的问题相匹配，那么过去的问题的影响是什么。这里的措辞非常经过深思熟虑。 我明确没有提及“如果问题被忽视可能会产生什么潜在影响”，因为这属于猜测/预测的范围。

在团队回顾期间，团队可以一起观看剪辑、提出问题并增加共享知识。 这样，团队中的每个人也会接触到更多几乎被忽略的错误。

为了避免出现频率差异，您可以将其限制为每人每次会议最多一个剪辑。

防火墙建模

在无需运行甚至查看代码的情况下查找错误（视频）（StrangeLoop 2019）中，Jay Parlar 描述了他尝试在 Alloy 中为访问控制系统构建模型的示例 - 该模型跨越多个代码库，并且他没有查看代码 - 在建模过程中，他发现了错误和设计问题。

根据我自己有限的经验，在尝试推理进程语义（涉及取消、潜在的无限期等待、文件锁定协议）以及访问控制时，轻量级形式方法似乎很有用。

作为基准，如果当您开始开发一个系统时，尤其是一个与多个外部系统交互或具有高安全性或正确性风险的复杂系统时，有两个人扮演建模者和程序员的角色，会怎么样？ 建模者可以在不查看代码的情况下开发模型，而程序员则可以处理代码。 他们会在中间会面创建测试用例。

然后，该模型可以作为一个更小的参考，以便能够检查代码的完整性，以及测试各种异常情况，否则需要大量的测试脚手架，尤其是在项目的早期阶段。

学习专业知识

（好吧，这个不属于“疯狂科学家”，但无论如何。 这是我的博客。）

在许多领域，围绕专业知识的文献越来越多。 对于代码（特别是代码审查）来说，这并不以完全相同的方式存在。

如果您分析了团队中发生的代码审查，并试图找出在富有洞察力的审查评论方面是否存在异常值（领域、人员）对，该怎么办？ 或者也许您只是通过采访人们获得了这些信息。

一旦发现异常值，您可以尝试一种易于学习的方法，例如应用认知任务分析，来提取这些人拥有的隐性知识。 与许多其他任务相比，这样做对于代码审查来说更容易，因为您实际上可以让人员实时审查 PR，而不是模拟难以模拟的情况（例如消防）。

围绕代码审查的时代精神

希望到目前为止，我已经让您相信审查代码是一项技能，并且我们还有更多的空间来尝试不同的实践。 例如，在训练计划方面，我们还没有接近更深入研究的领域，例如团队运动（例如足球）和两人游戏（例如国际象棋、围棋等）。

此时，您可能（合理地）仍在思考：“那又怎样？ 法学硕士在所有这些事情上做得比人类做得更好的速度要快得多，因此在审查代码方面尝试与法学硕士竞争是毫无意义的。”一个相关的反对意见可能是，虽然你可能关心代码审查，但你的管理层并不关心。 抱歉，我没有任何有关说服管理层的建议。

如果你还记得我之前的措辞：

如果您是一名软件开发人员，并且您相信在可预见的将来人们将继续参与程序的开发和维护，那么更好地审查代码就很有价值。

第二部分以第一部分为条件。 因此，我们可以不同意我们分配给前提本身的可能性（“如果你相信...... 在可预见的未来”）是正确的，但这与暗示（“然后”）本身是否成立是一个单独的讨论。

该含义的翻转版本将类似于：

如果您是一名软件开发人员，即使您相信在可预见的将来人们将继续参与程序的开发和维护，但更好地审查代码也绝对是负面的。

例如，你可以担任这个职位，因为你认为你可以学习其他技能，从而提供更高的影响力。我通常认为“系统设计”和“产品思维”或“培养品味”被吹捧为更重要的发展。 或者您可能认为审查代码以后将仅限于一小部分正在工作的程序员，就像今天相对一小部分程序员定期查看汇编代码一样。

对此，我有如下回应。

首先，如果与同行相比，你能够降低较低的抽象级别，那么这几乎总是一个优势，因为你能够解决比他们更广泛的问题。 例如，今天，如果您能够更轻松地理解 SQL 查询计划，或者您了解内存分配和汇编等内容，那么与不理解这些主题的工程师相比，您在设计更健壮和高性能的代码方面具有优势。

其次，考虑到与许多其他领域相比，软件开发仍处于起步阶段，我们很可能还没有接近看到人类技能和各个方面表现的上限，例如但不限于代码审查。 因此，你在周围看到的平均技能很可能远未达到上限。

最后，我建议您将世界观建立在经验报告、案例研究和您自己的观察中，而不是社交媒体上的“看法”。 Cedric Chin 在《如何理解人工智能》和《致一位担心人工智能的年轻人的信》中对此进行了比我更好的阐述。

归根结底，如果您要对您发布的代码负责，并且您发布的代码对真实的人产生真正的影响，那么值得问一下如何才能做得更好。 为此，我相信投资于更好地审查代码是作为软件开发人员可以做的最好的事情之一。
